titulo: Polyurethane plastic substitute can biodegrade in seawater, say scientists

fuente.nota: Text shortened by removing paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: On Thursday, September 22, scientists at the University of California San Diego reported in the journal Science of the Total Environment that a type of polyurethane already used in biodegradable land-based products can also break down when immersed in seawater. This polyurethane is already used as a substitute for plastic in foams and shoes.

The research team performed their experiments at the Ellen Browning Scripps Memorial Pier and Experimental Aquarium. They cut the polyurethane into cubes similar in size and shape to those naturally formed by EVA plastics. They wrote that several types of marine bacteria and fungi stick to the polyurethane and break it down to its component chemicals, which they then consume for food. The polyurethane microbes had already made detectable progress when the scientists checked the samples after four weeks in the water.

"Improper disposal of plastic in the ocean breaks down into microplastics and has become an enormous environmental problem," said study co-author Stephen Mayfield, director of the California Center for Algae Biotechnology. "We've shown that it's absolutely possible to make high performance plastic products that also can degrade in the ocean."

Humans deposit roughly 8 billion kg of plastic in the ocean each year, where it can be mistaken for food by marine organisms. Natural forces break the plastic into the small pieces that we call microplastic, while larger chunks form near-islands, such as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. By mass, about half the patch is commercial fishing waste, such as discarded nets, but reducing the amount of post-consumer plastic in the ocean would still make a considerable dent in the planet's plastic problem.
This type of polyurethane can be used to make flip-flops and parts of other shoes, which make up a large portion of the world's plastic waste.
titulo_es: A polyurethane plastic substitute can biodegrade in seawater, scientists say
resumen_es: Researchers at the University of California San Diego show that a polyurethane already used in foams and footwear breaks down in the sea thanks to bacteria and fungi, a possible help against plastic pollution.
nivel_motivo: The text is short and its technical vocabulary is limited and transparent for a Spanish speaker: C1 reflects its difficulty better than C2.

ideas_clave.idea: Researchers at UC San Diego have shown that a polyurethane already used as a plastic substitute in foams and shoes, and known to biodegrade on land, also decomposes in seawater.
In experiments at a pier and aquarium, marine bacteria and fungi colonised cubes of the material, broke it down and fed on it, with visible progress after only four weeks.
One of the authors argued that the study proves that high-performance plastic products able to degrade in the ocean can be made.

The problem is huge: billions of kilograms of plastic reach the ocean every year, harming marine life and forming microplastics and garbage patches, so cutting consumer plastic would make a real difference.
The material is suitable for flip-flops and other footwear, which account for a large share of the world's plastic waste.

resumen_modelo: The article reports that scientists at the University of California San Diego have found that a type of polyurethane, already used instead of conventional plastic in foams and shoes, can also biodegrade in seawater. In their experiments, cubes of the material were colonised by marine bacteria and fungi, which broke it down into its chemical components and consumed them, with noticeable results after just four weeks. According to one of the authors, this shows that high-performance plastic goods capable of degrading in the ocean are feasible. The finding is relevant because billions of kilograms of plastic end up in the sea every year, where they fragment into microplastics or accumulate in vast patches. Since footwear such as flip-flops represents a significant proportion of plastic waste, the new material could help reduce the problem.
